summary:
The IRS and forensic accountants use three court-accepted "formal indirect methods" to reconstruct and prove unreported income when books are absent, unreliable, or falsified: the Net Worth Method, the Source and Application of Funds (Expenditures) Method, and the Bank Deposits and Cash Expenditures Method. Each is codified for civil examiners in IRM 4.10.4 (Examination of Income) and for criminal special agents in IRM 9.5.9 (Methods of Proof). All three rest on the same economic identity — income must go somewhere: into assets, debt reduction, spending, or bank accounts — so unexplained accumulations, expenditures, or deposits in excess of reported and nontaxable funds are circumstantial evidence of unreported income. The constitutional blueprint is Holland v. United States, 348 U.S. 121 (1954), which upheld the net worth method in criminal tax prosecutions but imposed strict safeguards: the government must establish an opening net worth (a "firm starting point," including cash on hand) with reasonable certainty; must investigate and negate reasonable leads to nontaxable sources (cash hoards, gifts, loans, inheritances) that are reasonably susceptible of being checked; and must either show a likely source of taxable income or (per United States v. Massei, 355 U.S. 595 (1958)) negate all nontaxable sources. Holland also warned that the method is "fraught with danger for the innocent" and requires especially clear jury instructions explaining the method's assumptions and available inferences.

Mechanically: (1) Net Worth — ending net worth (assets at cost less liabilities) minus opening net worth = increase in net worth; add personal living expenditures and nondeductible losses/items; subtract nontaxable sources (gifts, inheritances, loan proceeds, nontaxable pensions, prior accumulated cash); compare the result (corrected adjusted gross income) to reported income; the excess is the understatement. (2) Source and Application of Funds (also called the Expenditures or T-account method) — total applications of funds (asset purchases, liability reductions, personal living expenses, other cash outlays) minus total known sources (reported income adjusted for non-cash items like depreciation, plus nontaxable receipts, loan proceeds, asset sales, decreases in assets, increases in liabilities) = understatement; it is arithmetically equivalent to a one-year net worth computation and works well for taxpayers who spend rather than accumulate. (3) Bank Deposits and Cash Expenditures — total deposits to all accounts, minus inter-account transfers and redeposits and other non-income deposits (loan proceeds, gifts, refunds, returned checks), equals net deposits from income; add cash expenditures not made from deposited/withdrawn funds (the "currency analysis" reconciling cash in vs. cash out, including cash on hand at start and end), subtract nontaxable cash sources, then compare to reported gross receipts; leading authority Gleckman v. United States, 80 F.2d 394 (8th Cir. 1935), and the method presumes deposits are income once the government shows an income-producing business/activity.

In litigation, the expert's product is a year-by-year schedule (the classic net worth statement with asset/liability line items at cost, yearly columns, and a bridge from net worth increase to corrected taxable income) supported by a workpaper trail tying every line to third-party documents (bank records, deeds, loan files, brokerage statements, BLS consumer expenditure data only as a floor for living expenses). Under Daubert/FRE 702 these methods survive challenge because they are long court-accepted, testable, documented in the IRM and published literature (peer review/general acceptance), and have known error-surfaces the expert must address — which is also the defense playbook: attack the opening cash on hand (cash hoard defense), assert nontaxable sources (loans, gifts, inheritances), attack asset valuation (must be cost, not FMV), duplicate-counting of transfers in bank deposit analyses, and failure to follow leads. Best practice — and the most persuasive courtroom presentation — is convergence: running two or three methods independently from the same records and showing the understatements corroborate one another within a narrow band, which rebuts the claim that the result is an artifact of any one method's assumptions.
key_points: Three formal indirect methods recognized by IRS and courts: (1) Net Worth Method, (2) Source and Application of Funds (Expenditures) Method, (3) Bank Deposits and Cash Expenditures Method — codified in IRM 4.10.4 (civil examination) and IRM 9.5.9 (criminal Methods of Proof). IRM 4.10.4 also lists the Markup Method and Unit and Volume Method as additional formal indirect methods, but the big three are the ones used to prove unreported income in court.

Net Worth formula (exact): Ending Net Worth (assets at COST basis − liabilities) − Beginning Net Worth = Increase in Net Worth; + Personal Living Expenditures + Nondeductible Losses/Items (e.g., capital losses in excess of limits, gifts made, federal income tax paid) = Total Net Worth Increase Plus Expenditures; − Nontaxable Sources (gifts received, inheritances, loan proceeds, insurance proceeds, nontaxable portion of pensions/Social Security, prior-accumulated cash) = Corrected Adjusted Gross Income; − Reported AGI = Understatement (unreported income). Assets must be at historical cost — unrealized appreciation is NOT income.

Holland v. United States, 348 U.S. 121 (1954) safeguards: (a) opening net worth must be established 'with reasonable certainty' — the firm starting point, critically including opening cash on hand; (b) government must show increases are attributable to currently taxable income — the 'likely source' requirement (e.g., an ongoing cash business); (c) government must investigate all relevant leads furnished by the taxpayer that are 'reasonably susceptible of being checked' — failure to negate reasonable explanations is fatal; (d) jury charges must be especially clear, summarizing the method, its assumptions, and inferences for and against the accused; the Court called the method one that is 'fraught with danger for the innocent.'

United States v. Massei, 355 U.S. 595 (1958): likely source is not indispensable — the government may instead negate ALL nontaxable sources of the net worth increase. Companion Holland-trilogy cases: Friedberg v. U.S., 348 U.S. 142 (opening net worth); Smith v. U.S., 348 U.S. 147 (corroboration of extrajudicial admissions); U.S. v. Calderon, 348 U.S. 160.

Cash-on-hand / cash hoard: in Holland the defense claimed a $104,000 pre-1933 currency hoard omitted from opening net worth; the government rebutted circumstantially (years of financial hardship, borrowing, installment buying inconsistent with holding a hoard). Standard rebuttal evidence: prior low reported income, loan applications and financial statements signed by the taxpayer showing low cash, bankruptcies, delinquencies, statements/admissions of cash on hand at interview.

Source and Application of Funds formula (exact): Total Applications of Funds (increases in assets + decreases in liabilities + personal living expenses + other nondeductible expenditures) − Total Known Sources of Funds (reported taxable income adjusted for non-cash deductions such as depreciation + nontaxable receipts + decreases in assets + increases in liabilities + beginning cash) = Understatement of Income. Also called the Expenditures Method or T-account method; it is a one-period cash-flow restatement of the net worth method; upheld in United States v. Johnson, 319 U.S. 503 (1943). Best for taxpayers who consume rather than accumulate.

Bank Deposits and Cash Expenditures formula (exact): Total Deposits to all accounts − Transfers between accounts − Redeposits of previously withdrawn cash − Other non-income deposits (loan proceeds, gifts, refunds, returned/NSF checks, counter credits from asset sales) = Net Deposits from Income; + Cash Expenditures made from undeposited receipts (business and personal expenses paid in currency, cash asset purchases) + increase in cash on hand − Nontaxable sources of cash = Total Receipts / Corrected Gross Income; − Reported Gross Receipts = Unreported Income. Leading case: Gleckman v. United States, 80 F.2d 394 (8th Cir. 1935), cert. denied 297 U.S. 709 (1936).

Transfer vs. deposit discipline: an inter-account transfer (check drawn on account A deposited to account B of the same taxpayer, or a redeposit of currency previously withdrawn) must be eliminated or income is double-counted — the single most common defense attack on a bank deposits case. The analyst must obtain ALL accounts (personal, business, spouse, nominee, brokerage) and trace every deposit item (deposit slips, deposited-items microfilm) to classify it as income, transfer, or non-income.

Currency (cash) analysis within the bank deposits method: Cash Available (cash on hand at start + cash receipts + cash withdrawn from banks) vs. Cash Applied (cash deposited/redeposited + cash expenditures + cash on hand at end). If cash spent exceeds known cash available, the excess is unreported cash income; this is the 'cash expenditures' add-on that captures skimmed currency never deposited.

Presumption structure: once the government proves the taxpayer had an income-producing activity and regular deposits, deposits are prima facie evidence of income and the burden of going forward shifts to the taxpayer to show non-income character (civil: Tokarski, DiLeo v. Commissioner, 96 T.C. 858 (1991); the IRS determination carries a presumption of correctness once a minimal evidentiary foundation linking taxpayer to income-producing activity exists).

Daubert/FRE 702 posture: these methods survive Daubert because they (a) rest on a testable accounting identity, (b) are published in the IRM, court opinions, and forensic accounting literature (peer review), (c) have decades of judicial acceptance (general acceptance since Capone-era prosecutions and Holland), and (d) their error sources are known and controllable (opening cash, transfers, nontaxable sources). Daubert exclusions of forensic accountants almost always stem from methodological shortcuts — unsupported assumptions, failure to verify starting balances, cherry-picked periods — not from the methods themselves. Expert must show reliable APPLICATION to the facts (FRE 702(d)).

Common defense attacks (each with the government/expert counter): (1) cash hoard — rebutted by financial history and admissions; (2) loans — demand notes, repayment evidence, lender's capacity and records; (3) gifts/inheritances — donor capacity, probate records, gift tax returns; (4) valuation errors — cost basis documentation; (5) unfollowed leads — the Holland leads doctrine; (6) double-counted transfers; (7) joint/commingled funds and nominee ownership; (8) prior-year (pre-period) income already taxed or barred by statute; (9) living-expense estimates (BLS tables) attacked as speculative — best practice is to build PLE from actual documented outlays and use BLS only as a conservative floor.

Corroboration/convergence: because all three methods are restatements of the same identity, running them independently (net worth for accumulation years, expenditures for consumption, bank deposits for deposit-heavy activity) and showing the annual understatements agree within a tight range is powerful triangulation; IRM and DOJ Tax Division practice is to use a second method as a check on the primary method, and courts treat convergence as strong evidence the result is not a computational artifact. Consistent year-over-year understatements across multiple years is itself evidence of willfulness (pattern evidence).

Classic net worth schedule layout the expert presents: columns = 12/31 of base year and each prosecution year; Section I Assets (cash on hand; cash in banks by account; inventory; loans/notes receivable; securities at cost; vehicles at cost; real estate at cost; business equipment; personal property; each with acquisition documentation), Total Assets; Section II Liabilities (mortgages, notes/loans payable, accrued depreciation reserve if assets shown gross, credit balances), Total Liabilities; Net Worth = I − II; prior column subtracted = Increase in Net Worth; Section III Add: personal living expenses (itemized: food, utilities, insurance, tuition, travel, federal/state income taxes paid, gifts made, nondeductible losses); Section IV Less: nontaxable sources (itemized with payor and date); = Corrected AGI (adjust for itemized deductions/exemptions to reach Corrected Taxable Income in a criminal case); Less reported income; = Understatement per year; with tax-due-and-owing computed per year for criminal counts.

When indirect methods are authorized: IRC §446(b) gives the Commissioner authority to compute income by any method that clearly reflects income when the taxpayer's method does not; IRM 4.10.4 requires a preliminary financial status analysis (cash-T) showing a reasonable likelihood of unreported income before a formal indirect method is used in a civil exam (RRA 1998 §7602(e) bars 'financial status' techniques absent such indication); indirect-method results are fully admissible in both civil deficiency and criminal evasion (§7201) cases.
terminology: Formal indirect method — an IRM-recognized technique for reconstructing income from circumstantial financial evidence rather than books and records (net worth, expenditures, bank deposits, markup, unit-and-volume).

Firm starting point / opening net worth — the reasonably certain statement of assets, liabilities, and cash on hand at the start of the first computation year, required by Holland; the anchor of any net worth case.
Cash on hand — undeposited currency held by the taxpayer; distinct from 'cash in banks'; the single most litigated line item because it drives the cash hoard defense.
Cash hoard defense — the claim that pre-period accumulated currency (not current income) funded the increases; rebutted circumstantially per Holland.
Likely source doctrine — Holland requirement that the government show a probable taxable source of the increases; alternative under Massei is full negation of nontaxable sources.
Leads doctrine — Holland duty to investigate taxpayer explanations 'reasonably susceptible of being checked'; unexplored plausible leads can defeat the case.
Personal living expenditures (PLE) — nondeductible consumption spending added back to net worth increase; documented item-by-item, with BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey data used only as a floor.
Source and Application of Funds / Expenditures method / T-account method — one-period cash-flow comparison of applications (uses) against known sources of funds; excess applications = understatement.
Net deposits — total bank deposits after eliminating inter-account transfers, redeposits, and non-income items; the income-indicative deposit base.
Transfer (inter-account) — movement of funds between the taxpayer's own accounts; must be eliminated to avoid double counting; distinguished from a true deposit of receipts.
Redeposit — currency previously withdrawn and returned to a bank account; a non-income deposit.
Currency (cash) analysis — reconciliation of cash available vs. cash applied to quantify unreported income spent in currency and never deposited (the 'cash expenditures' component).
Corrected adjusted gross income / corrected taxable income — the reconstructed figure produced by the indirect method, compared to per-return amounts to yield the understatement.
Tax due and owing — the criminal-case computation converting each year's understatement to evaded tax (element of IRC §7201).

Presumption of correctness / minimal evidentiary foundation — civil rule that the IRS deficiency determination stands once the government links the taxpayer to an income-producing activity (DiLeo; Tokarski).
Financial status analysis (cash-T) — preliminary IRM 4.10.4 comparison of known cash in vs. cash out used to justify deploying a formal indirect method (constrained by IRC §7602(e)).
Willfulness pattern evidence — consistent multi-year understatements shown by the schedules, supporting the intent element of evasion.
Convergence / corroboration of methods — independent computation under two or more indirect methods yielding materially consistent understatements, used to rebut method-artifact defenses.
Nominee ownership — assets titled in third parties (spouse, entity) but beneficially owned by the taxpayer; included in the net worth statement with attribution evidence.

Daubert / FRE 702 reliability factors — testability, peer review/publication, known error rate, general acceptance, and reliable application to case facts, all addressed in the expert's report for the chosen method.
demo_ideas: Interactive classic net worth schedule: a spreadsheet-style grid with years as columns (12/31/base through 12/31/final), asset/liability line items as rows, live-computed Net Worth, Increase in Net Worth, + PLE, − Nontaxable Sources, Corrected AGI, − Reported AGI, = Understatement rows highlighted — every cell click drills down to the underlying source document (deed, bank statement, loan file), mimicking the workpaper tie-out an expert presents at trial.

Three-method convergence dashboard: run Net Worth, Expenditures, and Bank Deposits computations off the same imported transaction set and display a grouped bar or bullet chart per year showing the three independently derived understatements landing within a tight band — the single most impressive 'triangulation' visual for a forensic accountant.

Bank deposit item classifier with an audit trail: ingest deposit-level data and let the user (or an auto-rule engine) tag each item as Income / Transfer / Redeposit / Non-income (loan, gift, refund), with a Sankey diagram flowing Total Deposits → eliminations → Net Deposits from Income → + Cash Expenditures → Corrected Gross Receipts, and a running double-count guard that flags matched withdrawal/deposit pairs across accounts.

Currency analysis T-account visual: side-by-side Cash Available vs. Cash Applied columns that reconcile to a highlighted 'unexplained cash expenditures' residual, with a slider for assumed opening cash on hand showing in real time how the cash hoard defense shrinks or erases the understatement — demonstrating sensitivity analysis the way a Daubert-ready expert would.

Holland safeguards checklist panel: for a loaded case, auto-score the government's proof against the Holland elements (firm starting point established? cash on hand corroborated? likely source shown or nontaxable sources negated? leads followed?) with green/amber/red status and citations — framing the tool as court-grade, not just arithmetic.

Defense-attack simulator: buttons to inject a claimed $100k cash hoard, an undocumented family loan, or an inheritance into the computation and watch each method's schedule recompute, paired with the rebuttal evidence the expert would need (loan applications, gift tax returns, probate records) — shows mastery of both sides of the courtroom fight.

Exhibit generator: one-click export of the year-by-year net worth schedule, the source-and-application statement, and the bank deposits summary as numbered trial exhibits (PDF) with a signed-workpaper index, matching the format of the appendix schedules in Holland-era prosecutions and modern IRS CI summary-witness exhibits.
